constitutive_assumptions: Steel and concrete display isotropic elastic behavior under serviceability limit state conditions (small deformation validity allowing superposition).
Steel beam and concrete slab cross sections remain planar before and after deformation (plane-section assumption).
Both materials possess an identical bending curvature.
Concrete slab uplift, lateral deformation, and steel-concrete interface friction are neglected.
Shear deformation is neglected in the theoretical derivation based on Euler-Bernoulli beam theory.
The relationship between interfacial longitudinal shear stress and slip follows a nonlinear model based on force and energy balance: Q/Qu = u / (a + u).
In the FE model, steel is modeled as an elastic-perfectly plastic material, and tension and compression behaviors are assumed identical.
Steel web is assumed to primarily resist the shear load.
control_variables: Beam span length and sectional geometric dimensions for each specimen series
Material elastic moduli of concrete (Ec) and steel (Es)
Total number of shear connectors (maintained constant when studying spacing ratios)
Static loading configuration (displacement-controlled midspan concentrated load)
dependent_variables: Bending deflection along the beam and at midspan (w)
Interfacial slip displacement along the beam and maximum slip at beam ends (u)
Bending strain distribution across the concrete slab and steel beam cross section (εc, εs)
Effective bending rigidity of the composite beam (Bs)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The effective bending rigidity of a layered composite beam considering nonlinear interfacial slip is analytically formulated between intuitive bounds of zero composite interaction and full composite interaction.

A closed-form analytical solution based on a trigonometric series and the principle of minimum potential energy predicts bending deflection within 3% of experimental values in the serviceability limit state.
Interfacial slip is antisymmetric about the load point, reaching zero at the midspan load application point and nonlinearly increasing to maximum values at the beam ends.

Conventional linear slip models substantially underestimate interfacial slip under higher load levels near the ultimate limit state, where end slip is 40% higher when considering interfacial nonlinearity.

Transverse shear deformation significantly alters deflection for low span-to-depth ratios (increasing deflection by 20% at L/H = 5), whereas Euler-Bernoulli assumptions neglecting shear deformation remain accurate for slender beams with L/H >= 10.
Unequal spacing of shear connectors has minimal impact (less than 5% variation in midspan deflection) compared to equal spacing when the total number of connectors is kept constant.

experimental_setup: Four simply supported steel-concrete composite beam test specimens (SCB-5, SCB-8, SCB-2, SCB-3) evaluated from literature (Yu et al. 2003; Huang et al. 2018).
Orthogonal concrete slab reinforcement with steel bars (HRB335) spaced at approximately 100 mm (10 mm diameter for SCB-5/SCB-8; 16 mm diameter for SCB-2/SCB-3).
Headed-stud shear connectors with diameters of 13 mm (SCB-5, SCB-8) and 16 mm (SCB-2, SCB-3).
Static concentrated midspan loading under displacement control.
Measurements of midspan deflection, longitudinal slip distribution along the interface, and cross-sectional bending strains.
independent_variables: Applied vertical load level and ratio to ultimate load (P, P/Pu)
Longitudinal location along the beam span (x/L)
Vertical position across the beam cross section (z, z')
Stud connector spacing and arrangement ratio (D1/D2 varied from 0.5 to 2.0)
Interfacial slip formulation (linear slip model vs. nonlinear slip model)
limitations_inferred: The derived closed-form solution is restricted to simply supported, single-span beams with symmetrical sections and does not cover multi-span, continuous, or geometrically complex structural systems.
The study investigates static monotonic loading and does not account for dynamic, cyclic, or fatigue degradation of shear connections.
The energy-based nonlinear slip equation requires parameter calibration (constant 'a') from physical push-out test data.
The research is strictly focused on civil structural steel-concrete beams and does not investigate or experimentally test robotic systems, soft actuators, or flexible continuum mechanisms.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The theoretical model assumes isotropic elastic behavior for both steel and concrete, which applies to serviceability limit states but does not represent material plasticity at ultimate limit states.
Effects such as concrete slab uplift, lateral deformation, and interface friction are neglected.
Shear deformation is neglected in the Euler-Bernoulli theoretical derivation, limiting its applicability to relatively slender beams with span-to-depth ratio L/H >= 10.
Reinforcement bars in concrete and interface friction were neglected in the finite element models.
The analytical derivation assumes equal stud spacing.
main_results: Derived an explicit closed-form analytical solution for deflection and interfacial slip of composite beams using a trigonometric series truncated at the first term.
Established a unified bending rigidity formula (Bs) that incorporates the nonlinear interface slip parameter.
Theoretical deflection predictions matched experimental measurements within 3% under serviceability loads (<= 0.5 Pu), and 3D nonlinear finite element results agreed within a maximum 5% difference.
Predicted cross-sectional bending strains matched experimental measurements within an 8% difference.
Nonlinear slip modeling predicted up to 40% higher maximum interfacial slip at the beam ends under high loading compared to conventional linear slip models.
Sensitivity analysis showed that unequal stud spacing ratios between 0.5 and 2.0 altered midspan deflections by less than 5%, confirming the validity of using average stud spacing.

Shear deformation increased deflections by up to 20% when the span-to-depth ratio dropped to L/H = 5, confirming that the Euler-Bernoulli analytical model is valid for slender composite beams with L/H >= 10.
modeling_methods: Variational principle (first-order variation of total potential energy)
Undetermined coefficient method using Fourier trigonometric series
Energy-based nonlinear shear load-slip interface model
Nonlinear 3D finite element modeling in ANSYS (SHELL181 for steel beam, SOLID65 for concrete slab, COMBIN39 for shear studs)
performance_metrics: Percentage difference between predicted (analytical and numerical) deflections and experimental deflections (3% for analytical, 5% for FE model)
Absolute difference between predicted interfacial slip and experimental measurements (maximum difference <= 0.02 mm under lower load)
Percentage discrepancy between predicted and experimental cross-sectional bending strains (< 8%)
Relative increase in maximum end slip between nonlinear and linear interface slip models (40% increase)
Deflection increase caused by shear deformation at low span-to-depth ratios (up to 20% increase at L/H = 5)
possible_gap_implications: The exact variational potential-energy framework and closed-form stiffness formulation for two-layer beams with nonlinear interfacial slip could potentially inform analytical modeling of multi-layer variable-stiffness continuum structures or laminar jamming mechanisms in mechanical engineering, but would require reformulation for large displacements, elastomeric material laws, and friction.
paper.research_objective: To propose and experimentally validate a closed-form, explicit, exact analytical model and a unified bending rigidity formula for bending deformation and interfacial slip in regular steel-concrete composite beams with partial shear connectors, accounting for interfacial nonlinearity.
paper.research_problem: Partial shear connections in steel-concrete composite beams result in inevitable interfacial slip and nonlinear structural behavior, particularly in the ultimate limit state where interfacial shear stiffness can be significantly reduced; however, existing design codes rely on oversimplified linear slip models that overestimate stiffness, while existing nonlinear analytical models are overly complex or depend on computationally intensive finite-element methods.
paper.title: Analytical Solution for Bending Deformation of Steel–Concrete Composite Beams Considering Nonlinear Interfacial Slip
